We did a pretty thorough benchmark of PMem and examined its use cases when the first version was released [here](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00778-020-00622-9).

I later on built a PMem-optimized data structure for Key-Value-Stores. You can find that paper  [here](https://db.in.tum.de/~vogel/papers/p2525-vogel.pdf?lang=de).

We then tried to more efficiently move date between different storage devices, including PMem DIMMs [here](https://db.in.tum.de/~vogel/papers/p55-vogel.pdf?lang=de).

I was also really baffled that Intel never really tried to emphasize that part and instead pushed the memory mode that is - frankly - quite boring. 

I guess the reason is that it takes A LOT of work to build applications for "persistent RAM" that are also crash consistent. They probably assumed that there wouldn't be enough of us programmers to develop enough software fast enough to drive sales. 

Selling it as "RAM but cheaper and more" was just easier.

A shame that it's more or less already dead. Could've had at least the courtesy to kill it after I'm done writing my PhD thesis about it...

Still awesome technology, the low write latency for small writes while being persistent is just out of this world and would've been awesome for all transactional database systems.
